messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai, an 18-year-old of South Eastern Asian heritage, presented with a pervasive sense of unease that had shadowed him since a traumatic event six months prior. He had been working as a freelance photographer, documenting the aftermath of a local conflict in his ancestral village, when his small group of aid workers was ambushed. The sudden eruption of gunfire, the screams, and the sight of those around him falling, left him paralyzed by a profound sense of helplessness. He vividly remembered the sounds of the struggle, the smell of dust and blood, and the agonizing belief that he should have been able to do something, anything, to protect the innocent people he was with.

Now, memories of that day feel "more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things," often striking "without warning" when he encounters everyday triggers. The sudden screech of tires on the street, the distant pop of fireworks, or even the smell of certain spices in a restaurant can instantly transport him back to the chaos. When these memories surge forward, Kai is overwhelmed by an intense "rage on recall" – a searing anger at the perpetrators, at the injustice, and at himself. This constant re-experiencing of the trauma, particularly the moments of his perceived inaction, relentlessly fuels his core belief that "I should have protected others and I failed." He has come to feel that "people can't be trusted," viewing the world through a lens of suspicion and danger, a conviction reinforced with every vivid, rage-filled recall of betrayal and loss. This profound conviction that he had failed and that others were untrustworthy seemed to prime his mind, pulling the most horrific details of the ambush to the forefront whenever his guard was down, as if to constantly remind him of the proof of his beliefs.

His conviction that "I should have protected others and I failed," coupled with the deep-seated belief that "people can't be trusted," has left Kai in a perpetual state of hypervigilance. He finds he "cannot relax even when I know I am in a safe place," his body tense, his senses scanning for threats. This constant internal alarm system manifests physically; he will "jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people," whether it's a door closing loudly in his apartment building or a sudden burst of laughter from passersby. As his internal state of threat has escalated, so too has his susceptibility to being triggered, making him more prone to those sudden, unwanted intrusions of memory. The sheer exhaustion of constantly being on guard has ironically led him to engage in "risky behavior," like driving at excessive speeds to get to a photoshoot or venturing into less safe areas for a unique shot, a desperate attempt to feel something other than dread, or perhaps an unconscious urge to test the very boundaries of the danger he perceives.

This pervasive sense of "threat," the unshakeable feeling that danger lurks everywhere, only solidifies Kai's cynical worldview. His inability to relax and his constant startle response confirm to him that "people can't be trusted" and that the world is inherently unsafe. He feels increasingly alienated, convinced that "I no longer belong anywhere," a painful consequence of both the trauma itself and his altered perspective. Once a passionate and meticulous photographer, his work has suffered. He finds himself avoiding certain urban environments that might contain triggers, and his "risky behavior" has led to several close calls, damaging both his equipment and his professional reputation. He sought help only when he realized he was trapped in a tightening loop, unable to escape the memories or the fear, longing for a way to simply breathe without the constant expectation of disaster.
